01.note: Issur and Rav Safra were business partners. Rav Safra dissolved the partnership without Issur's knowledge, in front of two witnesses, and came to Rabba bar Rav Huna, who told him to bring the court of three before whom he had divided it, or witnesses to that. Rabba bar Rav Huna cited the mishna that a stipulation is made before a court; Rav Safra answered that taking his own share was only making a fact known, for which two witnesses are enough, just as a widow sells estate property without a court. Abaye countered that even the widow needs a court of laymen. The text does not say how the case ended.
01.why: The mishna has just taught that a finder may make his condition about lost wages before a court; the story argues over whether that line proves a court is needed whenever one claims property tied up with someone else's.

people.name: Issur
people.about: Rav Safra's partner in a joint business venture.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Issur's partner, who split their property without telling him.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage Rav Safra came to, who demanded a court of three.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Challenges Rav Safra's proof from the widow.

terms.meaning: The core collection of early rabbinic law; the Gemara is the later discussion built around it.
The smallest Jewish court, made up of three judges, needed for many legal acts.
A court of three ordinary people rather than ordained expert judges.

02.note: Rav Hisda asked his teacher Rav Huna what the law is for a student whose teacher needs him. Rav Huna took the question as being about himself and said: Hisda, Hisda, I do not need you; you need me for forty years. The two grew angry and stopped visiting each other. Rav Hisda observed forty fasts because Rav Huna had been offended, and Rav Huna observed forty fasts because he had wrongly suspected Rav Hisda.
02.why: The Gemara is asking which teacher's lost item a person must return before his own father's; Rav Hisda's question extends that to a student who is also his teacher's study partner.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rav Huna's disciple and study partner, who asked the question.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rav Ḥisda's teacher, who took offense at the question.

terms.meaning: Days of fasting taken on as an act of regret and atonement.

03.note: A man left jewels with another for safekeeping. When he asked for them back, the keeper said he did not know where he had put them. Rav Nahman ruled that saying I do not know is itself negligence and ordered him to pay. When he did not pay, Rav Nahman had his palace seized to cover the jewels. Later the jewels turned up, and they had risen in value. Rav Nahman ruled that the jewels go back to their owner and the palace goes back to its owner.
03.why: Right after it, Rava asks why the keeper did not keep the jewels, like a bailee who pays instead of swearing, and explains that this keeper had forced the owner into court, so the rule does not apply.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who ordered payment and then reversed the seizure.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.
Careless guarding. A bailee who was negligent must pay for what was lost.

04.note: Some gardeners used to leave their spades every day with a certain old woman. One day they left them with one of the gardeners instead. He heard the noise of a wedding, went out to it, and left the spades with the old woman. While he was away, the spades were stolen. Rav exempted him from paying.
04.why: Rav and Rabbi Yohanan dispute whether a bailee who hands a deposit to another bailee is liable. Rav Hisda says Rav's view was only inferred from this ruling, wrongly: here the owners themselves used to leave their spades with her.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who exempted the gardener.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Explains what Rav's ruling in this case did and did not mean.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.

05.note: An old woman with three daughters was taken captive together with one daughter. Of the other two, one died and left a young son. Abaye asked who should hold the old woman's property: not the surviving sister, since the old woman may be dead and the boy an heir; not the boy, since she may be alive. He ruled half to the sister and a steward for the other half; Rava said a steward for all of it. Later word came that the old woman had died. Abaye gave a third to the sister, a third to the boy, and split the captive daughter's third between the sister and a steward; Rava again said a steward for the whole of that third.
05.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a court never puts a relative in charge of a minor's property, lest he later be taken for its owner; this case works that rule out when the heirs are a child and a captive.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Works out how to divide the captive woman's property.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Holds that a steward should manage every uncertain share.

terms.meaning: A guardian appointed by the court to manage property for someone who cannot, such as a child or a captive.
A court letting a relative take over and work someone else's property while the owner is absent or too young.

06.note: A man from Bei Hozai came to the wealthy Mari bar Isak, said he was his brother, and demanded half the inheritance; Mari said he did not know him. Rav Hisda told the man to bring witnesses, but the man said they feared Mari, a violent man, so Rav Hisda made Mari prove the man was not his brother, over Mari's protest. Witnesses came and confirmed the brother, who then claimed half of the orchards Mari had planted as well, and Rav Hisda agreed, citing a mishna about older brothers who improve shared property. Rabba agreed, Abaye questioned it, and Rabbi Ami said Mari should be paid for his work. After messages went back and forth, Rabbi Ami learned the brother had been a minor and conceded that Rav Hisda was right.
06.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a court never lets a relative manage a minor's property; Rav Hisda's final answer rests on that rule, since Mari worked the land without court approval while his brother was a minor.

people.name: Mari bar Isak
people.about: A wealthy and violent man whose unknown brother claimed a share of the inheritance.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: The judge in the case.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Agrees that the improvements are shared.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Questions whether the mishna fits Mari's case.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Argues Mari should be paid for his work, then concedes.

terms.meaning: A place far from where Mari lived, which is why the brothers did not know each other.

terms.term: the burden of proof rests upon the claimant
terms.meaning: The usual rule that whoever wants to take property from another must prove his claim.
Someone who works another's field for a share of the crop; here the measure for paying a relative who tended property.
The core collection of early rabbinic law; the Gemara is the later discussion built around it.

07.note: A man left money with another for safekeeping, and the keeper put it in a hut made of willow branches, from which it was stolen. Rav Yosef ruled the keeper liable: the hut was safe against thieves but careless against fire, so the loss began with negligence and ended by accident. Others report the ruling the other way, as exempt. The Gemara concludes that the keeper is liable.
07.why: The Gemara has been listing where money must be hidden to count as properly guarded; this case asks about a spot that is safe from one danger but not from another.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the stolen money.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.

terms.term: initially through negligence and ultimately by accident
terms.meaning: A loss where the keeper was careless, but the item was in the end lost in a way his carelessness did not cause.

08.note: A man left money with another for safekeeping. When he asked for it back, the keeper said he did not know where he had put it. The case came before Rava, who ruled that saying I do not know is itself negligence, and told the keeper to pay.
08.why: It is one of a run of cases on how a keeper must guard deposited money; this one sets the rule that a keeper who cannot say where he put it counts as negligent.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who ordered the keeper to pay.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.
Careless guarding. A bailee who was negligent must pay for what was lost.

09.note: A man left money with another for safekeeping. The keeper gave it to his mother, who put it in a chest, and it was stolen. Rava asked how judges should rule in such a case. His answer is not given here.
09.why: It is one of a run of cases on guarding deposited money; this one asks whether a keeper may hand a deposit to a family member.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Asks how the case should be judged.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.

09.flag: The story stops at Rava's question; his reasoning and ruling follow in the next segments, which are a separate story entry (2A4A44).

10.note: A keeper gave deposited money to his mother, who put it in a chest, and it was stolen. Rava weighs each side. The son can say that anyone who deposits something expects the keeper's wife and children to help guard it. The mother can say her son never told her the money was not his, or she would have buried it. And the son can say he kept quiet because she would be more careful with money she thought was his. Rava's ruling follows after this.
10.why: Rava is working out who, if anyone, must pay; these arguments clear both son and mother of negligence, leading to his ruling that both swear an oath and the son is exempt.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Weighs the claims of the keeper and his mother.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.

10.flag: Starts mid-case: the facts and Rava's question are in the preceding entry (BFE58A), and the ruling is in the AFTER segment; the STORY holds only the argument.

11.note: A steward who managed the affairs of some orphans bought them an ox and handed it to a cowherd. The ox had no molars or other teeth to eat with, and it died. Rami bar Hama asked how judges should rule in such a case. His answer is not given here.
11.why: It follows a case where a keeper passed money to his mother; here too a loss passed through several hands, and the Gemara asks which of them, if any, must pay.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: Asks how the case should be judged.

terms.meaning: A guardian appointed to manage property for someone who cannot, here for orphans.

11.flag: The story stops at Rami bar Hama's question; the reasoning and ruling are in the AFTER segments.

12.note: A man left hops, used in brewing beer, with another man who had a pile of hops of his own. The keeper told his brewer to use hops from this pile, but the brewer went and used the other pile, the deposited hops. Rav Amram asked how judges should rule in such a case. His answer is not given here.
12.why: It is the next in a run of cases where a deposit is lost through someone the keeper relied on, and the Gemara asks who must pay.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: Asks how the case should be judged.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.

12.flag: The story stops at Rav Amram's question; the reasoning follows in the AFTER segments.

13.note: Rav Pappa had twelve thousand dinars owed to him in Bei Hozai. He transferred them to Rav Shmuel bar Aha by giving him the threshold of his house, so the coins passed to him along with the land. When Rav Shmuel bar Aha came back, Rav Pappa went out as far as Tevakh to meet him.
13.why: The Gemara has just concluded that coins cannot be acquired by a symbolic exchange; it notes that Rav Pappa, who had held they could, changed his mind, as shown by his using land to transfer these coins.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Owner of the money, who transferred it to Rav Shmuel bar Aḥa.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Aḥa
people.about: The man Rav Pappa sent to collect the money.

terms.meaning: A way of handing over movable things, such as coins, by attaching them to a transfer of a piece of land, here the threshold of a house.
A distant place where the money was owed.
A symbolic way of completing a deal, usually by handing over a cloth.

14.note: Buyers paid Rabbi Hiyya bar Yosef for salt. Then the price of salt rose, and he wanted to back out. He came to Rabbi Yohanan, who told him: go and give them the salt, and if not, accept upon yourself He Who exacted payment. The Gemara then retells the case: the money was only a down payment, Rabbi Hiyya bar Yosef thought it bought salt worth just that much, and Rabbi Yohanan told him it bought the whole order.
14.why: Abaye says one who reneges is only warned with He Who exacted payment; Rava says he is cursed and cites this case. The Gemara rejects the proof and recasts it as a case about down payments, opening the dispute that follows.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Cites the incident as proof for his view.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage who sold salt and wanted to back out when its price rose.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage he asked, who told him to deliver the salt.

terms.meaning: A formula from the mishna: the One who punished the generation of the flood and others will punish whoever does not keep his word. It is said to someone who backs out of a paid deal.
Part of the price paid up front to bind both sides to a deal.

15.note: Buyers paid Rav Kahana for linen. Then the price of linen rose. Rav Kahana came to Rav, who told him to give the buyers linen worth the money he had received; for the rest, his promise was only words, and going back on words alone is not bad faith.
15.why: The Gemara has been asking whether a down payment secures the whole deal or only its own worth; Rav's ruling follows the second view, and it introduces the dispute over whether breaking a spoken promise is bad faith.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who took money for linen and wanted to back out when the price rose.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who ruled on Rav Kahana's case.

terms.meaning: Breaking trust; going back on a commitment others relied on, which the Sages disapprove of even when the law cannot force it.

16.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya told his son to go and hire workers. The son agreed to feed them, without saying what food. When he came back, his father told him that even a feast like King Solomon's would not fulfill the duty, since they are descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Instead, before they began work, the son was to tell them they could claim only bread and legumes.
16.why: The Gemara is debating whether going back on a spoken promise is bad faith; it calls this an older dispute of the tanna'im, then asks how Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya could tell his son to change the terms.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Matya
people.about: The father, who sent his son to hire workers.

people.name: his son
people.about: Hired the workers and promised them meals.

terms.meaning: The Sages of the Mishna period, earlier than the Sages who debate in the Gemara.
The core collection of early rabbinic law; the Gemara is the later discussion built around it.

17.note: A man paid in advance for sesame. Then the price of sesame rose, and the sellers backed out: we have no sesame, take your money. He did not take it, and the money was stolen. Rava ruled that once they told him to take his money and he did not, the sellers were not even unpaid keepers of it. The Sages asked Rava whether the sellers still had to accept He Who exacted payment, and he said they did.
17.why: The Gemara has just argued that Rabbi Yohanan treats backing out of a spoken deal as bad faith; this case adds the risk for money a buyer leaves with sellers who back out.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge in the case.

terms.meaning: Two levels of keeper. A paid keeper must pay if the item is stolen; an unpaid one only if he was careless.
A formula from the mishna: the One who punished the generation of the flood and others will punish whoever does not keep his word. It is said to someone who backs out of a paid deal.

18.note: Rav Pappi reports from Ravina what Rav Tavot (some say Rav Shmuel bar Zutra), a man who would not bend the truth for the whole world, told him. One Friday at twilight a man stood at his door and asked if he had sesame to sell; he said no. The man asked to leave his dinars with him, since it had grown dark, and he answered: this house is before you. The man put the money in the house and it was stolen. Rava ruled that whoever says this house is before you is not even an unpaid keeper. Ravina asked about the Sages telling Rava that the seller must accept He Who exacted payment, and Rav Tavot said that never happened.
18.why: It follows the sesame case where Rava's ruling ended with the Sages demanding the curse; this eyewitness account places Rava's ruling in a different setting and denies the curse was ever raised.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Passes on the account he heard from Ravina.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Heard the account and asked about the Sages' remark.

people.name: Rav Tavot
people.about: A scholar famed for honesty who tells of what happened to him; some name him Rav Shmuel bar Zutra.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge in the case.

terms.meaning: Someone who keeps another's property as a favor; he must pay only if he was careless.
A formula from the mishna: the One who punished the generation of the flood and others will punish whoever does not keep his word. It is said to someone who backs out of a paid deal.
Friday at dusk, when the man could no longer carry money or get home before the Sabbath.

19.note: A man paid in advance for wine. Then he heard that men from the house of Parzak the vizier wanted to seize it. He told the seller: give me my money, I do not want the wine. The case came before Rav Hisda, who said that just as the Sages made pulling complete a sale for sellers, so they made it complete a sale for buyers.
19.why: The Gemara has been explaining why the Sages ruled that pulling the goods, not paying, completes a sale; Rav Hisda applies that rule to a buyer who wants out before taking the goods.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: The judge in the case.

people.name: Parzak
people.about: A vizier whose men wanted to seize the wine.

terms.meaning: Physically drawing goods into one's possession, the act the Sages made the step that completes a purchase of movable goods.

20.note: Rami bar Hama's landlord sold a donkey at a wrong price and was sad about it. Rami bar Hama asked why, heard what had happened, and told him to go and undo the sale. The landlord said too much time had passed, longer than it takes to show the goods to a merchant or a relative. Rami bar Hama sent him to Rav Nahman, who said that time limit applies only to a buyer; a seller may always back out.
20.why: The Gemara is discussing how long buyer and seller may undo a sale made at the wrong price, and why the merchants of Lod rejected Rabbi Tarfon's longer limit; this case sets the seller's rule.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: A Sage who noticed his landlord's distress.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage who ruled that a seller may always back out.

terms.term: time to show to a merchant or relative
terms.meaning: The mishna's limit for undoing a sale at an unfair price: only as long as it takes to show the goods to someone who knows the market.
